It handles detection, OCR, counting, segmentation and alpha matting in one model, with a 9.6M-parameter pixel decoder. The post Tencent WeVisOne-VL Unifies Detection, OCR, Segmentation and Matting appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Tencent’s WeChat Vision team has released WeVisOne-VL , an open vision language model in 2B and 4B sizes. The WeVisOne-VL vision language model handles detection, referring, counting, pointing, OCR, segmentation and alpha matting in one model. Pixel outputs come from a 9.6M-parameter decoder, so no separate SAM is needed. It also answers “None” when a queried object is absent. For developers, that can replace a detector, an OCR engine and a segmenter with one model. TL;DR Size: 2B ( 2.44B params ) and 4B ( 4.83B params ) on Hugging Face, and a 9.6M-parameter pixel decoder. Trained with up to 8,192 tokens of context; deployment context length is not disclosed. Runs on: A single GPU through Transformers or vLLM in BF16. The package also lists NPU and CPU devices. VRAM needs are not disclosed. A community GGUF ran object-level tasks on a 6 GB RTX 2060. Performance: Beats the same-scale VLM baselines in Tencent’s tables on most of 30+ benchmarks (self-reported). Best: 71.3 F1 Mean on Dense200 dense detection, versus 58.7 for LocateAnything-3B. Worst: 52.6% rejection rate on PR-Bench, so many absent-target queries still get a box. What is WeVisOne-VL? WeVisOne-VL (“WeChat Vision All-in-One”) is a perception-focused model from Tencent built on Qwen3-VL . It targets fine-grained localization rather than open-ended chat. Users choose the output granularity: points, boxes, binary masks or continuous alpha mattes. How does WeVisOne-VL work? Every task is cast as structured next-token prediction. The model adds coordinate tokens <0> to <1000> for normalized boxes and points. An absent target produces None instead of a guessed box. For pixel tasks, the model emits an <OBJ> token after each predicted box. Its hidden state becomes a query for the pixel decoder, according to the model card . The decoder has 3 parts: Visual Feature Adapter: reuses multi-level Qwen3-VL ViT features instead of a second image encoder. Box-Guided Query Decoder: 6 deformable cross-attention blocks seeded by the <OBJ> state and the box. Dense Prediction Head: refines output at S/4, S/2 and S/1 into a full-resolution mask or matte. How was it trained? A knowledge-graph-driven data engine annotated over 100M images with about 3.6B boxes. SAM3, Rex-Omni and an in-house detector proposed regions, and Qwen3-VL verified them. Training used 3 SFT stages. Stage 1 aligned output formats on 90M examples. Stage 2 raised input to 1,960 visual tokens and up to 500 boxes per response. Stage 3 trained the pixel decoder, then specialized it for matting on 130M samples. A final GRPO stage used 178K uncertainty-filtered examples, as described in the research paper . How does WeVisOne-VL perform on benchmarks? All numbers below are self-reported, using greedy decoding and at most 1,960 visual tokens per image. Detection, referring and OCR use F1 averaged over IoU 0.5 to 0.95. Detection: 55.3 F1 on LVIS and 71.3 on Dense200 for the 4B model. Referring: 81.8 F1 on RefCOCOg test, versus 77.6 for LocateAnything-3B. Rejection: 96.4% on Tencent’s in-house WeRef-Bench (2,880 queries), versus 73.0%. Counting: 89.6% exact-match on PixMo-Count test, versus 82.8%. OCR: 52.0 F1 on TotalText, ahead of the PP-OCRv5 specialist at 25.7. Segmentation: 71.2 gIoU on ReasonSeg val, versus 65.0 for LISA-13B. Matting: 7.3 MAD on P3M-500-NP box prompts, versus 15.4 for SAM2-Matting (SAM3). Lower is better. The 2B model trails the 4B model on most tasks. It still scores better box-prompted matting on P3M-500-NP, at 6.6 MAD. WeVisOne-VL vs Qwen3-VL, Rex-Omni and LocateAnything Feature WeVisOne-VL-4B Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct Rex-Omni LocateAnything-3B Developer Tencent WeChat Vision Alibaba Qwen IDEA Research NVIDIA Size 4.83B (HF listing) 4B 3B (card) 3B (card) Base model Qwen3-VL Not applicable Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct + MoonViT-SO-400M License Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 IDEA License 1.0 NVIDIA non-commercial Native masks / mattes Yes (9.6M decoder) Not in model card Not in model card Not in model card Context Not disclosed (8,192 in training) 256K native Not disclosed Not disclosed LVIS F1 Mean 55.3 44.0 46.9 50.7 Dense200 F1 Mean 71.3 15.2 58.3 58.7 RefCOCOg test F1 Mean 81.8 74.3 74.3 77.6 RefCOCOg-Rej rejection 67.4% 18.8% 0.5% 0.6% PointBench 71.9 57.1 69.9 56.9 TotalText F1 Mean 52.0 33.0 40.6 43.3 How do you run WeVisOne-VL? Weights for the 2B and 4B models are on Hugging Face. The wevisone_vl package wraps Transformers and vLLM backends. Tasks include detection , referring , point , count_box , ocr , segmentation and matting . from wevisone_vl import WeVisOneVL model = WeVisOneVL("tencent/WeVisOne-VL-4B", backend="transformers") # or "vllm" result = model.predict(image, task="matting", query="person") Hosted demos are live for 2B and 4B . Tencent also open-sourced Mask2Alpha , the matting annotator from its data engine. Fine-tuning code is still on the TODO list. GGUF builds cannot produce masks, since the decoder needs native visual features. Key Takeaways 1 model covers detection, OCR, counting, pointing, segmentation and matting. A 9.6M-parameter decoder replaces SAM for masks and alpha mattes. 4B scores 71.3 F1 on Dense200, 12.6 points above LocateAnything-3B. Apache 2.0 weights, unlike non-commercial LocateAnything-3B. Check out the Paper , GitHub repo , Model weights and Project page . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . It posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and 81.6 on LiveCodeBench, but trails similar-size models on knowledge benchmarks. The post webAI Releases TwIL-8B, an 8.8B Reasoning Model Scoring 98.2 on MATH-500 appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> webAI has released TwIL-8B , an 8.8B reasoning model for math, code and instruction following. The TwIL-8B reasoning model is post-trained from IBM’s Granite 4.2 8B . Weights are on Hugging Face under a non-commercial license. webAI’s launch post frames the pitch around cost per task, not raw scale. The 4-bit build is 4.98 GiB, sized for CPU or modest-VRAM GPU inference. TL;DR Size: 8.79B parameters, dense. 131,072-token context, inherited from the base model. Runs on: CPU or modest-VRAM GPU via a 4.98 GiB Q4_K_M GGUF. Full bf16 weights are 16.38 GiB. Performance: Leads its size class on math and code, trails on knowledge benchmarks. Best: MATH-500 at 98.2, the top score in webAI’s comparison. Worst: GPQA Diamond at 70.2, 11.5 points behind Qwen3.5-9B. HLE is 12.6 (verbose variant). What is TwIL-8B? TwIL-8B is a dense decoder-only reasoning model from webAI. It has 40 layers, hidden size 4096, and 32 attention heads with 8 KV heads . Input and output are English text only. The model writes a <think> block before each answer. It ships in 2 variants with the same architecture and tokenizer. Balanced is the default and produces shorter reasoning traces. Verbose reasons longer and targets hard contest-style problems. TwIL-8B extends webAI’s TwIL family. The first members were 1.7B and 3B formal-logic models released in August 2026. How was TwIL-8B trained? webAI used 3 post-training stages : Full-parameter SFT on reasoning traces for math, STEM and instruction following. GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning on math, code, STEM and instruction prompts. This produces the verbose variant. Length-aware RL with a reward that favors shorter traces against per-domain length references. This produces the balanced variant. Training pools were decontaminated with 13-gram matching against AIME, HMMT, MATH-500, GPQA and other evals. How does TwIL-8B perform on benchmarks? All TwIL-8B scores are self-reported, high-effort pass@1 with thinking enabled. Scores marked † were measured on the verbose variant only. Math : TwIL-8B scores 98.2 on MATH-500. Qwen3.5-9B lists 96.6 on a third-party leaderboard . Gemma 4 31B scored 87.9 in Red Hat’s lighteval run . On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B posts 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On AIME 2026 it scores 88.3, behind Qwen3.5-9B at 92.5 and Gemma 4 31B at 89.2 . Code : LiveCodeBench† is 81.6, against 65.6 for Qwen3.5-9B and 80.0 for Gemma 4 31B. webAI notes its LiveCodeBench version was not recorded. Competitor scores are v6. Instruction following : IFBench† is 74.4, 9.9 points above Qwen3.5-9B at 64.5. IFEval is level, at 91.8 vs 91.5. Knowledge : This is the weak spot. GPQA Diamond is 70.2, against 81.7 for Qwen3.5-9B and 84.3 for Gemma 4 31B. MMLU-Pro† is 76.5 vs 82.5 for Qwen3.5-9B. Across 13 shared benchmarks, TwIL-8B goes 7-6 against Qwen3.5-9B. Against Gemma 4 31B, about 3.5x its size, it goes 3-11. Does TwIL-8B use fewer reasoning tokens? Yes, against its closest open peer. On AIME 2026, TwIL-8B averages about 19.5k output tokens per problem. Qwen3.5-9B uses 31.2k, so TwIL-8B uses 38% fewer. It scores 4.2 points lower. On HMMT Feb 2026 the gap is 32.9k vs 40.6k, or 19% fewer. Frontier models remain far leaner. webAI cites about 5k tokens per AIME 2026 problem for GPT-5.5. webAI states that harnesses and tokenizers differ, so treat this as directional. TwIL-8B vs Qwen3.5-9B vs Gemma 4 Metrics TwIL-8B Qwen3.5-9B Gemma 4 12B Gemma 4 31B Parameters 8.79B dense 9B (language model) 11.95B dense 30.7B dense Context 131,072 262,144 native 256K 256K Modality (input) Text Text, image, video Text, image, audio Text, image License webAI Non-Commercial 1.0 Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 Smallest official local build 4.98 GiB (Q4_K_M) Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed MATH-500 98.2 96.6 (3rd party) Not disclosed 87.9 (Red Hat) AIME 2026 88.3 92.5 (MathArena) 77.5 89.2 LiveCodeBench 81.6 † 65.6 (v6) 72.0 (v6) 80.0 (v6) GPQA Diamond 70.2 81.7 78.8 84.3 MMLU-Pro 76.5 † 82.5 77.2 85.2 TwIL-8B figures from the model card . † = verbose variant. All scores self-reported by each vendor unless marked. How do you run TwIL-8B locally? from_pretrained("webAI-Official/TwIL-8B") loads the balanced variant. Pass subfolder="verbose" for the verbose one. The model card lists GGUF builds for llama.cpp: Q4_K_M, 4.98 GiB, for both variants Q8_0, 8.70 GiB, verbose only F16, 16.38 GiB, verbose only Give it a large generation budget. The card’s example sets max_new_tokens=32768 . A short budget truncates reasoning and scores far worse. All reported scores used bf16 weights, so expect small drops at Q4_K_M. No hosted inference provider serves the model on Hugging Face yet. Key Takeaways TwIL-8B is an 8.79B dense reasoning model post-trained from IBM Granite 4.2 8B. It posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and 81.6† on LiveCodeBench. It uses 38% fewer tokens than Qwen3.5-9B on AIME 2026. Knowledge is weak: GPQA Diamond trails Qwen3.5-9B by 11.5 points. Weights are open but licensed for non-commercial use only. Check out the model card and weights on Hugging Face and webAI’s announcement on X . The post webAI Releases TwIL-8B, an 8.8B Reasoning Model Scoring 98.2 on MATH-500 appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> webAI has released TwIL-8B , an 8.8B reasoning model for math, code and instruction following. The TwIL-8B reasoning model is post-trained from IBM’s Granite 4.2 8B . Weights are on Hugging Face under a non-commercial license. webAI’s launch post frames the pitch around cost per task, not raw scale. The 4-bit build is 4.98 GiB, sized for CPU or modest-VRAM GPU inference. TL;DR Size: 8.79B parameters, dense. 131,072-token context, inherited from the base model. Runs on: CPU or modest-VRAM GPU via a 4.98 GiB Q4_K_M GGUF. Full bf16 weights are 16.38 GiB. Performance: Leads its size class on math and code, trails on knowledge benchmarks. Best: MATH-500 at 98.2, the top score in webAI’s comparison. Worst: GPQA Diamond at 70.2, 11.5 points behind Qwen3.5-9B. HLE is 12.6 (verbose variant). What is TwIL-8B? TwIL-8B is a dense decoder-only reasoning model from webAI. It has 40 layers, hidden size 4096, and 32 attention heads with 8 KV heads . Input and output are English text only. The model writes a <think> block before each answer. It ships in 2 variants with the same architecture and tokenizer. Balanced is the default and produces shorter reasoning traces. Verbose reasons longer and targets hard contest-style problems. TwIL-8B extends webAI’s TwIL family. The first members were 1.7B and 3B formal-logic models released in August 2026. How was TwIL-8B trained? webAI used 3 post-training stages : Full-parameter SFT on reasoning traces for math, STEM and instruction following. GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning on math, code, STEM and instruction prompts. This produces the verbose variant. Length-aware RL with a reward that favors shorter traces against per-domain length references. This produces the balanced variant. Training pools were decontaminated with 13-gram matching against AIME, HMMT, MATH-500, GPQA and other evals. How does TwIL-8B perform on benchmarks? All TwIL-8B scores are self-reported, high-effort pass@1 with thinking enabled. Scores marked † were measured on the verbose variant only. Math : TwIL-8B scores 98.2 on MATH-500. Qwen3.5-9B lists 96.6 on a third-party leaderboard . Gemma 4 31B scored 87.9 in Red Hat’s lighteval run . On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B posts 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On AIME 2026 it scores 88.3, behind Qwen3.5-9B at 92.5 and Gemma 4 31B at 89.2 . Code : LiveCodeBench† is 81.6, against 65.6 for Qwen3.5-9B and 80.0 for Gemma 4 31B. webAI notes its LiveCodeBench version was not recorded. Competitor scores are v6. Instruction following : IFBench† is 74.4, 9.9 points above Qwen3.5-9B at 64.5. IFEval is level, at 91.8 vs 91.5. Knowledge : This is the weak spot. GPQA Diamond is 70.2, against 81.7 for Qwen3.5-9B and 84.3 for Gemma 4 31B. MMLU-Pro† is 76.5 vs 82.5 for Qwen3.5-9B. Across 13 shared benchmarks, TwIL-8B goes 7-6 against Qwen3.5-9B. Against Gemma 4 31B, about 3.5x its size, it goes 3-11. Does TwIL-8B use fewer reasoning tokens? Yes, against its closest open peer. On AIME 2026, TwIL-8B averages about 19.5k output tokens per problem. Qwen3.5-9B uses 31.2k, so TwIL-8B uses 38% fewer. It scores 4.2 points lower. On HMMT Feb 2026 the gap is 32.9k vs 40.6k, or 19% fewer. Frontier models remain far leaner. webAI cites about 5k tokens per AIME 2026 problem for GPT-5.5. webAI states that harnesses and tokenizers differ, so treat this as directional. It beat the best InferenceX configurations by up to 2.6x TPS in under 24 hours per model. The post Together AI Releases Together Compiler: Agents Make Inference Up to 2.6x Faster appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Together AI has introduced Together Compiler (TKCC), an agent-driven system that keeps re-optimizing inference as production traffic changes. Together Compiler already runs on several of Together’s serverless endpoints. The core claim for developers: an engine tuned once goes stale, so tuning should never stop. TL;DR System: It is an optimization system, tested on Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash and Llama 1B. Runs on: NVIDIA B200, B300, GB300, H100, AMD MI355X and AWS Trainium2. Each run used at most 2 nodes per model. Performance: Up to 2.6x higher TPS than the best published InferenceX configurations, in under 24 hours per setting. Best: 1,111 P90 TPS per user on MiniMax M3.1 Flash (B200, batch size 1), 1.8x over the 633 TPS baseline. Worst: GLM 5.3 on MI355X moved only from 463 to 480 TPS (about 4%). What is Together Compiler? Together Compiler is a continual compilation loop from Together AI that uses coding agents to rewrite a model’s forward pass. It takes a server launch command, a traffic profile and a hardware configuration. Agents propose faster forward passes, and a persistent engine measures each one. The winning code ships into the serving engine. When traffic drifts, the loop runs again. Why does inference need continual compilation? Together AI team reports that its traffic shape never sits still. Prompt lengths in one country ran about 97K tokens versus 70K elsewhere. One customer’s P90 input length grew from 18K to 33K tokens in 3 days. Kernels tuned on random data can also mislead. Random inputs activated 13 to 38% more MoE experts than real traffic. One agent-written top-k kernel took 20 µs on random data. On real data at 70K context, it took up to 62 ms. How does the persistent engine work? Most agent loops restart vLLM, SGLang or TensorRT-LLM for every experiment. The research team measures 761 seconds of cold startup for MiniMax M3.1 Flash on TensorRT-LLM. Together Compiler starts the engine once. Agents submit a candidate forward pass over RPC. The server swaps the forward function pointer and re-captures CUDA graphs. Two measurement tiers balance speed and fidelity. A fast tier serves 12 layers for quick screening. A slow tier serves 60 layers to confirm gains on real distributions. Two tiers tested 8.1x more candidates than one slow tier (1,354 vs 168). They also found a solution 7.2% faster. Together AI team reports 252x higher agent experiment throughput than an engine-restart baseline. How does it choose a parallelism layout? A cost model ranks tensor, expert, data and context parallel layouts before agents start. It mixes spec-sheet numbers, microbenchmarks and measured forward passes. It also uses measured MoE expert imbalance and uneven request lengths. On Kimi K3, it found a production layout with up to 24% higher TPS. What did agents need from human experts? An expert-curated knowledge base produced 25 to 31% lower speedup after 12 hours. Naive agents told to make the forward pass “as fast as possible” beat expert strategies. The ensemble scores were 6.2x versus 4.9x after 10 trials. Custom logging structures ate up to 43% of tool calls. Together AI now gives agents raw engine source code, not an intermediate representation. Benchmarks: how fast is Together Compiler? On SemiAnalysis InferenceX ‘s AgentX workload, Together Compiler beat the best open configurations by up to 2.6x TPS. Each setting ran under 24 hours on at most 2 nodes. Batch size 1, P90 TPS per user (Together Compiler vs InferenceX best, self-reported): MiniMax M3.1 Flash (B200): 1,111 vs 633 DeepSeek v4.1 Flash (GB300): 1,205 vs 943 GLM 5.3 (B200): 417 vs 329 Kimi K3 (GB300): 450 vs 423 GLM 5.3 (MI355X): 480 vs 463 For MiniMax, the cost model picked TP8 over the baseline’s TP4. That halves each GPU’s weight traffic in memory-bound decode. On Llama 1B at batch size 1, it beat Hazy Research megakernels , Mirage and CUDA-graph baselines by up to 1.7x. Beyond LLMs, it sped up 8 scientific models by 1.5x to 6.4x with bit-exact outputs. Claude Code with /goal reached 1.2x to 4.4x and failed on AIFS-ENS 2.0. oldContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Wed, 04 Nov 2026 19:48:20 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.12 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Crunchbase Data: Less Than 2% Of 2026 Venture Funding Went To Post-Election Red States https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/2026-post-election-funding-red-states-drops/ Wed, 04 Nov 2026 19:47:54 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94324 For the past few decades, the vast majority of U.S. startup funding has consistently gone to companies in blue states or purple states, where Democrats control all or some statewide offices. But with Tuesday’s election results, the investment divide between blue, purple and red states has grown even more pronounced. So far this year, less than 2% of all startup investment has gone to companies in post-election red states, defined as those that will have both a Republican governor and two Republican U.S. senators. The red states’ share is much smaller than in years’ past due to five states shifting to purple. Of those, the largest venture hub is Texas, which shifted to purple with the election of Democratic Senator James Talarico and Governor Gina Hinojosa, followed by Ohio. This year, as of Election Day, startups in the remaining 17 red states 1 , which are home to nearly a quarter of Americans, had collectively pulled in just $8.6 billion in venture funding, with Florida, Tennessee and Utah among the largest contributors. To put that in perspective: It’s less than the typical nationwide total in a single week. Purple states rising The 10 purple U.S. states 2 , meanwhile, are home to just over a quarter of Americans and pulled in about $28.6 billion this year as of Election Day. That’s much higher than the red state tally, but still less than 6% of all U.S. startup funding. Beyond the aforementioned newcomers Texas and Ohio, several other purple states regularly pull in sizable venture funding, including Pennsylvania, North Carolina and to some extent Wisconsin. Also worth noting: The divide between red, purple and blue states is somewhat less stark when it comes to round counts. About 12% of startup financings of $1 million or more went to purple state companies this year, and about 9% went to red states. Broadly, it looks like backers are still finding plenty of investment-worthy talent outside of blue states when it comes to smaller deals. However, they are concentrating most of their capital into big AI rounds for California and New York companies. Blue states get over 90% of startup funding This brings us to our next point: Blue states receive the overwhelming majority of startup funding, of which most goes to California. 3 Per a Crunchbase analysis last week, California companies had pulled in more than three-fourths of all U.S. startup funding in 2026. Most of that stems from mega-financings for San Francisco-based OpenAI and Anthropic . While no other state comes close to California for attracting investment, the nearest runners up are also predominantly blue states, including New York and Massachusetts. In total, blue states have pulled in a staggering $481 billion in startup investment this year as of Election Day, per Crunchbase data, a new record. Politics and what makes for a venture hub So is it politics, or coincidence? Broadly speaking, the qualities that geographic startup hubs share — such as a deep tech talent pool, urban environs, leading tech companies and top research universities — aren’t specifically the domain of blue states. That said, predominantly rural states, which tend to lean red, are less likely to have those ingredients. Even so, there’s no rule against red state startup prowess. Austin, for example, managed to cement its status as a major tech hub even while Texas remained solidly under Republican control. And Utah also boasts a sophisticated startup scene. But following a Democratic electoral sweep, it’s hardly a surprise that more startup hubs now find themselves located in blue or purple states. newContent: Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ Data-driven reporting on private markets, startups, founders, and investors Thu, 05 Nov 2026 16:51:00 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.8.12 https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/cb_news_favicon-150x150.png Crunchbase News https://news.crunchbase.com/ 32 32 Exclusive: Nurx And Journey Clinical Co-Founders Raise $6M For Mental Health Startup Siggy https://news.crunchbase.com/venture/nurx-journey-clinical-founders-raise-mental-health-startup-siggy/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 16:00:40 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94329 Siggy has raised $6 million in pre-seed funding to build a mental health service that uses AI to collect patients’ histories and track progress between appointments with licensed clinicians, the startup told Crunchbase News exclusively. The company brings together two founders who previously built businesses that help patients get treatment outside a traditional doctor’s office. Jonathan Sabbagh co-founded Journey Clinical , which supports practices offering ketamine-assisted psychotherapy, and Edvard Engesæth co-founded Nurx , which provides birth control and other healthcare services online. Village Global led the financing for New York-based Siggy. Notably, several investors in the round previously backed one or both founders. They include Albert Wenger of Union Square Ventures , Mercury co-founder Immad Akhund , and Cityblock Health co-founder Toyin Ajayi , through Coalition Operators . Other participants include PsyMed Ventures , Mystic Ventures and Gokul Rajaram . Jonathan Sabbagh and Edvard Engesæth, co-founders of Siggy. (Courtesy photo) The founders said they began building Siggy in late 2025. The round, which they plan to use to hire more clinicians and engineers, develop the software and work on regulatory requirements, is the first outside funding for the company. The startup recently began accepting paying patients ahead of its public launch, and the founders said they next plan to test the service with paying patients before expanding further. Between appointments Sabbagh, Siggy’s CEO, told Crunchbase News in an interview that the company is addressing a problem he encountered in mental healthcare. Therapists and the clinicians prescribing their patients’ medication often work separately. Patients may see a therapist weekly but have only a brief appointment every few months with their prescriber. This leaves little time or opportunity to discuss changes in symptoms or medication side effects. To address that problem, Siggy uses AI conversations and daily check-ins to gather information clinicians can review between visits. “AI helps maintain the conversation and organize what patients share, so clinicians have a richer picture of the person that they’re treating,” said Engesæth, the startup’s COO, in an interview. Patients begin by answering questions about their history through a free AI conversation. They then meet a licensed clinician by video, who reviews that information. The clinician then makes a diagnosis and prescribes medication if appropriate. Patients can talk with Siggy’s AI between appointments and can also check in each day to report their sleep, mood, medication and how they feel physically. The company combines those answers with data from connected wearable devices to produce a daily “Siggy Score” out of 100. The score is visible to both the patient and clinician. Patients can opt to connect wearables such as Whoop , Oura or Apple Watch, adding sleep, activity, heart rate and heart rate variability data to the daily check-ins that underpin the Siggy Score. The company aims to use those patterns to flag difficult stretches earlier, including when patients report feeling fine despite worsening sleep or other physical changes. If the score changes, the software flags it for a clinician to review. Patients also receive weekly check-ins during their first eight weeks of treatment, according to the company. Clinicians decide whether to continue treatment or adjust medication, and also handle all medical questions. When appropriate, they can help patients taper off gradually. Siggy does not prescribe controlled substances and is not a crisis service, the founders said. One important note: Patients can continue seeing their existing therapists while using Siggy, Sabbagh said. A planned feature would let patients share information with other providers and involve loved ones in their care. A prior working relationship As with many startup founders, Sabbagh’s interest in mental health treatment grew out of his own experience. After two decades in finance, he experienced burnout and was eventually diagnosed with PTSD related to childhood trauma. He said ketamine-assisted therapy helped him recover, leading him to return to school to study psychology at 38. He subsequently co-founded Journey Clinical. Sabbagh said he has since become its executive chairman, remaining involved while taking on the CEO role at Siggy. Engesæth, a physician by training, was an early investor in Journey and advised Sabbagh as he built the company. Before that, Engesæth co-founded Nurx, which initially helped patients obtain birth control prescriptions and receive medication at home. He said the company grew to more than 2 million patients and an annual revenue run rate exceeding $100 million before merging with Thirty Madison in 2022. The two had considered starting a company together for years. With Siggy, they say they want to make the regular contact and coordination Sabbagh had with his own providers available to more patients. Accepting insurance Siggy accepts commercial insurance in all 50 states and is expanding into government insurance programs. Patients can also pay directly; insured patients’ costs vary by plan. Insurance was a priority because many prospective patients cannot afford treatment out of pocket, Engesæth said. The founders also say Siggy’s service will be permanently free to veterans. Investor POV Amrit Rao , a general partner at Village Global, told Crunchbase News via email that the founders’ experience building healthcare companies was a major reason he invested. The fact that Siggy accepts insurance was important too. “Pairing that vision with an insurance-based model makes the ambition about access as much as technology,” he said. Mercury co-founder and CEO Immad Akhund, who invested personally, is a repeat backer of both founders. He pointed to their longer-term ambition of using AI to understand each patient’s brain health well enough to detect changes early. “That’s why I’m backing them again with Siggy,” he added, “and why I’m excited to be in early on what they build next.” Related Crunchbase query: Global Venture Funding To AI Healthcare Companies In 2026 Illustration: Dom Guzman ]]> https://news.crunchbase.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/Mental_Health_App.png Dropbox Plans $350M AI Infrastructure Deal With Tigris Buy, Its Biggest Acquisition Yet https://news.crunchbase.com/ma/dbx-ai-infrastructure-deal-tigris-acquisition/ Thu, 05 Nov 2026 14:00:20 +0000 https://news.crunchbase.com/?p=94328 Dropbox announced Thursday plans to acquire Tigris Data for $350 million in a transaction the company told Crunchbase News would mark its largest acquisition since its founding in 2007.
